analysis.one_liner: Exempts certain commissioned sales employees from federal overtime and wage recordkeeping rules.
analysis.headline: The bill cleared a House subcommittee on an 8-6 vote in June 2001, then died in the full committee without ever reaching a House vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would change the Fair Labor Standards Act, the law that sets the federal minimum wage and requires overtime pay after 40 hours a week. It would remove those overtime and wage-recordkeeping requirements from sales employees who have specialized product knowledge, sell mainly to existing customers, and earn a base salary of at least one and a half times the minimum wage (annualized) plus commissions equal to at least 40 percent of that base. Route sales drivers, like delivery drivers who also sell, would be explicitly excluded.
analysis.who_benefits: Employers with specialized sales forces gain the most: they would no longer owe time-and-a-half for long hours worked by qualifying salespeople and would no longer have to keep wage-and-hour records for them. Covered salespeople would get one thing in return — a guaranteed base salary floor and a commission structure written into law — but would give up overtime pay.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Employers of specialized commissioned sales staff

how_it_helps.text: Qualifying sales employees would be exempt from the Fair Labor Standards Act's minimum-wage recordkeeping and overtime requirements.

To qualify, the employee must receive base compensation of at least one and a half times the federal minimum wage multiplied by 2,080 hours, with additional commission-based pay of at least 40 percent of that base amount.
Employers would be freed from the recordkeeping paperwork the wage-and-hour law otherwise requires for covered employees.

analysis.who_pays: Covered sales employees bear the cost: they would lose the right to overtime pay after long weeks and the wage-and-hour records that make enforcement possible. Workers pushed into the category but who don't truly fit it — for example, employees whose 'specialized knowledge' is thin or whose commissions fall short in practice — would lose protections without gaining much.

drawbacks.text: Exempted employees would lose the right to time-and-a-half overtime pay, so employers could require long hours at no extra cost.
The exemption also removes wage-and-hour recordkeeping requirements, leaving workers with less documentation of hours actually worked if a dispute arises.

The qualifying tests are self-applied by employers based on job descriptions, creating a risk that employees who do not truly match the profile — high-commission inside sales, for example — get reclassified out of overtime protections.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: There is a real trade here: a guaranteed base salary plus commission floor (1.5x minimum wage annualized, with commissions at 40 percent or more) is a meaningful guarantee for some salespeople, and the carve-out for route sales drivers protects a vulnerable group. But the core effect is narrowing overtime coverage, and the loss of recordkeeping requirements weakens the main tool workers have to prove hours worked. The bill was modest in scope — it touched only a slice of sales jobs — but what it did touch, it took away from workers.

outcome.mechanism: A House subcommittee approved it on a narrow 8-6 vote in late June 2001 and sent it to the full Education and Workforce Committee, which never took it up, and it died when that Congress ended in January 2003.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on June 6, 2001, by Rep. Patrick Tiberi together with Rep. Robert Andrews, a Democrat, and referred to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce.
It was sent to the Subcommittee on Workforce Protections, which held a markup on June 27, 2001, and forwarded it to the full committee on a party-close 8-6 vote.
The full committee never held a markup or sent the bill to the House floor, and no further action was recorded before the 107th Congress ended on January 3, 2003.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Sales workers in the affected positions kept their federal overtime rights and wage-and-hour recordkeeping protections. Employers did not get the exemption they sought, and the bill's sponsors got nothing for their effort.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Sales workers who kept overtime rights

for.name: Rep. Patrick J. Tiberi

against.name: House Committee on Education and the Workforce

against.name: Rep. John Boehner

sides.party_line_note: A Republican sponsored the bill but a Democrat co-introduced it, cosponsors split 4 Democrats to 7 Republicans, and the subcommittee vote was close at 8-6, so the fight did not break cleanly by party.

industries.industry: Employers of specialized commissioned sales staff (business-to-business sales, financial services sales, technical product sales)
industries.note: The bill would have freed these employers from paying time-and-a-half for long hours and from keeping wage-and-hour records for qualifying salespeople, shifting hours costs onto the workers themselves. The guaranteed base-pay floor was the offset offered to workers, but the exemption itself is an employer gain at employee expense.

industries.industry: Route sales distribution (beverage, snack, and bakery route drivers)
industries.note: Route sales drivers were expressly carved out of the exemption, so their employers would have gained nothing from the bill even if it had passed. From the workers' side, the carve-out preserved their overtime rights.
